title: Pop Tarts: No Fruit Necessary
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (credited in transcript as "iHeart Intro" for Chuck's lines) trace the history of Pop-Tarts, from the 1960s Kellogg and Post toaster pastry race through the Heckman Biscuit partnership, the 1964 launch and Cleveland test market, flavor and frosting development, spin-offs and failed products, marketing and mascots, the fire hazard and lawsuits, the "made with real fruit" controversy and health critiques, pop culture appearances, and ways to eat them. The episode ends with a listener mail about a remote control game show project.

segments.title: Opening banter and grandmothers
segments.summary: Hosts banter about grandmothers and pop tarts, then introduce the topic of pop tart origins and the 1960s context of convenience food.

segments.title: Kellogg and Post cereal origins
segments.summary: Background on the Kellogg brothers' Battle Creek Sanitarium, C.W. Post's cereal company, and the growth of the breakfast cereal market leading companies to seek new convenience foods.

segments.title: Post's Country Squares
segments.summary: Post develops foil-wrapped fruit pastries and announces Country Squares in 1963 via the Battle Creek Enquirer, prompting rivals to catch up.

segments.title: Kellogg, Heckman partnership and first flavors
segments.summary: Kellogg's develops its own version with the Heckman Biscuit Company in Grand Rapids; recipe testing leads to scoring the dough, and the original flavors with Smucker's fillings are set.

segments.title: Buttered Pop-Tarts tip and flavor preferences
segments.summary: Hosts discuss favorite flavors and Chuck's tip of buttering Pop-Tarts after toasting.

segments.title: Original design, two-pack packaging, and name change
segments.summary: Early Pop-Tarts were rounder and unfrosted, sold two per package for cost reasons, and renamed from Country Squares' competitor to Pop-Tarts in a nod to pop art.

segments.title: Launch, Cleveland test market, and product line growth
segments.summary: Trademark filed in 1964, shipping started September 1964 with Cleveland as test market and strong sales; Post's brand was sold in 1971; competitors like Toaster Strudel and frosting debut in 1967; sales growth and market share.

segments.title: Side products: Danish Go Round
segments.summary: Kellogg's Danish Go Round, replaced by Danish Rings, and a short note about Danish pastries.

segments.title: Presto Pizza and pie irons
segments.summary: Presto Pizza, a 1971 pizza version that failed for being too doughy, and a comparison with campfire pie irons.

segments.title: Hot foods and eating out of the foil
segments.summary: Hosts compare pop tarts with hot pockets and pizza rolls, and discuss eating pop tarts straight from the foil.

segments.title: Marketing, mascots, and Pop-Tarts Bowl
segments.summary: Pop-Tarts marketing to kids, Milton the Toaster mascot, Crazy Good slogan, campaigns, the Pop-Tarts Bowl, spin-off company, and the giant party pastry.

segments.title: Pop-Tarts fires, Dave Barry column, and lawsuit
segments.summary: Reports of toaster fires from Pop-Tarts, including Dave Barry's 1993 column, a flame experiment, a Consumer Product Safety Commission count, and a 1995 settlement.

segments.title: Made with real fruit lawsuit and health critiques
segments.summary: Nutrition facts of frosted strawberry Pop-Tarts, the children's advertising review unit challenge over 'made with real fruit,' the 2021 class action dismissed by a federal judge, and differences in European and UK ingredients.

segments.title: Cultural references and flavors
segments.summary: The Netflix movie Unfrosted, homemade pop tarts, Afghanistan food drops, Simpsons appearance, PB and J and wacky flavors, and the sugar cookie flavor.

segments.title: Survey stats and mystery flavor
segments.summary: Survey statistics about why people buy Pop-Tarts, the 2021 mystery everything bagel flavor campaign, and closing plans to buy boxes.

segments.title: Listener mail: Remote Control game show
segments.summary: Listener Michelle shares a childhood story about making a Remote Control-style game show project about Mesopotamia in 1990.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask for childhood sweet memories and sign off.
